extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and standard proof techniques for comparing sizes of sets (finite, denumerable, uncountable) using bijections, injections, surjections, the pigeonhole principle, diagonalisation, and listing arguments. Suitable for constructing or checking proofs about cardinality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite set cardinality via bijection to {1,...,n}
rubrics_metrics.description: When we write |A| = n ∈ N, we are really stating that there is a bijection f : A → {1, 2, 3, . . . , n}. Counting a finite set is constructing a bijection to an initial segment of the natural numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting can be formalised as constructing a function that is injective (different objects map to different numbers) and surjective (every number gets used). Special case: when A = ∅ we write |A| = 0 and treat separately since domain cannot be empty for a function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equinumerous sets / definition of same cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets A, B are said to have the same cardinality (or same cardinal number), written |A| = |B|, if either A = B = ∅ or there is a bijection from A to B. If A and B have the same cardinality then we say they are equinumerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition allows comparing sizes of finite and infinite sets via existence of bijections; non-equinumerous means no bijection exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of cardinality is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: For sets A, B, C: |A| = |A| (reflexive); if |A| = |B| then |B| = |A| (symmetric); if |A| = |B| and |B| = |C| then |A| = |C| (transitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use identity function for reflexivity, inverse of a bijection for symmetry, and composition of bijections for transitivity. Useful for showing two sets have same size by relating both to a third set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality inequalities via injections and surjections
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B is an injection then |A| ⩽ |B|. If g : A → B is a surjection then |A| ⩾ |B|. If h : A → B is a bijection then |A| = |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrapositives/alternative forms: for finite sets, if |A| > |B| then any function f : A → B cannot be injective; if |A| < |B| then any f : A → B cannot be surjective. Composition of injections (or bijections) preserves the relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (Dirichlet's Schubfachprinzip)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n > 0 objects are placed in k > 0 boxes then: if n < k then at least one box has zero objects in it; if n > k then at least one box has at least two objects in it. More precisely, in the second case at least one box contains at least ⌈n/k⌉ objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrapositive or contradiction proofs. Many combinatorial arguments reduce to placing objects in boxes; apply this to functions between finite sets to deduce impossibility of injections/surjections when sizes mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of infinite set (Dedekind)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is infinite when there is a bijection between A and a proper subset of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the bijection f(n)=2n shows N is equinumerous with the even numbers E, a proper subset of N. This captures 'infinite' without reference to natural-number counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denumerable / countable / uncountable definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is denumerable if there is a bijection f : N → A. The cardinal number of a denumerable set is denoted ℵ0. A set A is countable if it is finite or denumerable. A set is uncountable if it is not countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently there is a bijection from A to N iff from N to A. Denumerable sets can be 'listed' as an infinite sequence without repetition where every element appears at some finite position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing characterization of denumerable sets (Lemma 12.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is denumerable iff one can construct an infinite list a1, a2, a3, ... of all its elements such that the list does not repeat and any given element appears at some finite position in the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a bijection f:N→A set an=f(n) to obtain the list. Conversely, given such a list define g(n)=an to obtain a bijection. These two properties (no repeats; every element appears finitely) are both necessary and sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsets of denumerable sets are countable
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is denumerable and B ⊆ A then B is countable (either finite or denumerable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If B is infinite, index the positions of elements of B in a listing of A to produce a bijection from N to B (order the index set I = {n | a_n ∈ B} as i1<i2<...).

rubrics_metrics.name: kZ, kN and n^2-type infinite subsets are denumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: For any k ∈ N the sets kZ = {kn | n ∈ Z}, kN = {kn | n ∈ N}, and {n^2 | n ∈ N} are denumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are infinite subsets of a denumerable set (Z or N), so apply the previous theorem; explicit bijections can also be constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product of denumerable sets is denumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are denumerable sets then A × B is denumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a bijection by arranging ordered pairs in an infinite grid and enumerating them by sweeping successive diagonals (the standard diagonal/snake enumeration). Note that enumerating by columns or rows alone would fail to be surjective because some columns/rows are never reached in finite time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive rationals Q+ are denumerable (and hence Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of positive rational numbers is denumerable: list rationals in an infinite table a/b and enumerate by diagonal sweeps, skipping duplicates (fractions with common divisors). Then extend to Q by interleaving positives and negatives and 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative injection: map each reduced fraction a/b (a,b∈N, gcd=1) to the pair (a,b) in N×N to obtain an injection; its range is an infinite subset of N×N so denumerable. When listing by diagonals, remove repeats to ensure injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union and intersection of countable sets are countable
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countable sets then A ∪ B and A ∩ B are also countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by cases: intersection is subset of A so countable; union: if disjoint and infinite, interleave listings (a1,b1,a2,b2,...); if not disjoint, partition B into C=B−A which is disjoint from A and apply previous case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence and transference of cardinality inequalities (Remark 12.1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties analogous to integer equality: |A| ⩽ |A|; (|A| ⩽ |B|) ∧ (|B| ⩽ |A|) ⇒ (|A| = |B|); (|A| ⩽ |B|) ∧ (|B| ⩽ |C|) ⇒ (|A| ⩽ |C|). The middle one is the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First follows from identity injection; compositions of injections give transitivity. Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein requires a separate (nontrivial) proof (see Section 12.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument setup for uncountability of (0,1)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show (0,1) is uncountable assume for contradiction there is a bijection f : N → (0,1) and list the decimal expansions of f(1), f(2), ... in an array. Use properties of decimal expansions (rationals have repeating expansions; some have two expansions — choose the expansion ending in zeros) to normalise representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the diagonal ∆ whose nth digit is the nth digit of f(n). From ∆, build a number z whose nth digit differs from the nth digit of ∆; z differs from every f(n) in at least the nth decimal place, so z is not in the list, contradiction. Take care about ambiguous decimal expansions by choosing canonical expansions (ending in zeros).

rubrics_metrics.name: If A ⊆ B and A uncountable then B uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subset A of B is uncountable then B must also be uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove the contrapositive: if B is countable (finite or denumerable) then every subset is countable. Use this when deducing uncountability of larger sets from known uncountable subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive listing warnings / pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing enumerations of infinite sets (e.g. A × B or Q+), naive row- or column-wise listings may fail to reach elements in other columns/rows in finite time and so not yield a surjective map from N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagonal/sweep enumerations or interleaving techniques that ensure every element is reached after a finite number of steps; when duplicates arise (e.g. non-reduced fractions), explicitly skip repeated entries to ensure injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of explicit bijections and constructive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many cardinality results are established by explicitly constructing bijections (or injections/surjections) between sets, or by producing listings that define such maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, give an explicit formula or algorithm (e.g. explicit f(n) for Z or N×N enumeration) so the bijection is clear; otherwise give constructive listing or diagonal argument. Proof sketches should indicate how to construct the required mapping and check injectivity/surjectivity.
